claim: Seawater samples were collected twice a month from 11 coastal sites for 2 years between August 2017 and August 2019 at the Boso Peninsula, Japan, totaling 550 samples.
source: We collected seawater samples twice a month (i.e., around the first and second quarter moons) for 2 years between August 2017 and August 2019 at the 11 sites.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sampling frequency, duration, number of sites, and total sample count in the Methods section.

claim: The study region is located on the Pacific side of Honshu Island around 35°N and is markedly affected by the warm Kuroshio Current, cold Oyashio Current, and inner-bay water from Tokyo Bay.
source: This region is located on the Pacific side of Honshu Island around 35°N and is markedly affected by the warm Kuroshio Current, cold Oyashio Current, and inner-bay water from Tokyo Bay.
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the geographic location and oceanographic characteristics of the study region.

claim: eDNA metabarcoding detected 856 MOTUs across 33 orders, 167 families, and 466 genera.
source: We inspected their family-level phylogenies to increase the accuracy of taxonomic assignments, recognizing 856 MOTUs across 33 orders, 167 families, and 466 genera (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific numbers of taxonomic units detected through the eDNA metabarcoding analysis.

claim: The taxonomic diversity detected by eDNA was similar to that of the local fauna compiled from literature survey and museum collections (948 species across 33 orders, 158 families, and 493 genera).
source: This taxonomic diversity was similar to that of the local fauna (948 species across 33 orders, 158 families, and 493 genera) compiled from a literature survey and museum collections (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The manuscript compares the eDNA-detected diversity with known local fauna diversity from literature and museum records.

claim: Acanthopagrus schlegelii eDNA was detected in 504 out of 550 water samples (91.6%).
source: Metabarcoding detected the eDNA of A. schlegelii in 504 out of 550 water samples (91.6%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and, thus, we decided to use the sequence reads of A. schlegelii as the internal standard DNA of each sample.
evidence: The manuscript reports the detection frequency of A. schlegelii and references a figure showing this data.

claim: Fish eDNA concentrations and fish species richness showed a clear intra-annual pattern (seasonality), being higher in warmer months than in colder months at all sites.
source: Fish eDNA concentrations and fish species richness showed a clear intra-annual pattern (i.e., seasonality; Figure 1b, c), which were higher in warmer months (e.g., between July and October) than in colder months (e.g., between January and March) at all sites.
evidence: The manuscript describes seasonal patterns in eDNA concentrations and species richness, referencing figures that show this data.

claim: Total eDNA concentrations and species richness positively correlated with water temperature.
source: Total eDNA concentrations and species richness positively correlated with water temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states a positive correlation and references a figure showing this relationship.

claim: The negative controls produced negligible reads (177 ± 665 reads [mean ± standard deviation]), accounting for ca. 0.1% of the positive sample reads.
source: The negative controls produced negligible reads (177 ± 665 reads [mean ± standard deviation]), which accounted for ca. 0.1% of the positive sample reads.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific quantitative data on contamination levels in negative controls.

claim: All reads from negative controls were assigned to non-target taxa, such as fish species that had never been observed in the study region and freshwater fish species.
source: Moreover, all of the reads were assigned to non-target taxa, such as fish species that had never been observed in the study region and freshwater fish species (possibly contaminated from the laboratory).
evidence: The manuscript describes the taxonomic assignment of reads from negative controls.

claim: The top 50 most frequently detected species had detection frequencies ranging between 148 and 532 with a mean of 296.
source: The detection frequencies of these 50 species ranged between 148 and 532 with a mean of 296, and their total detection frequencies reached 14,793 (62.0% of the total detection frequency).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistics on detection frequencies for the top 50 species.

claim: The total detection frequencies of the top 50 species reached 14,793, representing 62.0% of the total detection frequency.
source: The detection frequencies of these 50 species ranged between 148 and 532 with a mean of 296, and their total detection frequencies reached 14,793 (62.0% of the total detection frequency).
evidence: The manuscript reports the cumulative detection frequency and percentage for the top 50 species.

claim: At the regional scale, the linear correlations among water temperature, total eDNA concentrations, interaction strengths, the number of interactions, and species richness were all statistically clear (p < 0.05) except for the linear correlation between water temperature and mean interaction strengths (p > 0.05).
source: At the regional scale, the linear correlations among water temperature, total eDNA concentrations, interaction strengths, the number of interactions, and species richness was all statistically clear (p < 0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) except for the linear correlation between water temperature and mean interaction strengths (p > 0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical significance of correlations and references a figure showing these relationships.

claim: Interaction strengths became weak as species richness increased.
source: The interaction strengths became weak as species richness increased, which is consistent with a previous study (Ratzke et al., 2020; Ushio, 2022a), suggesting that understanding the causes and effects of weak interactions is key to understanding the maintenance of species-rich communities.
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between interaction strengths and species richness, citing previous studies.

claim: The largest information flow was detected from Pseudoblennius marmoratus to Pseudolabrus eoethinus.
source: The largest information flow was detected from Pseudoblennius marmoratus to Pseudolabrus eoethinus (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The manuscript identifies the strongest detected interaction between two specific species.

claim: Bidirectional information flow was detected between Pseudolabrus eoethinus and Gymnothorax kidako.
source: Bidirectional information flow was detected between P. eoethinus and Gymnothorax kidako.
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific bidirectional interaction between two species.

claim: In-strengths and out-strengths of fish species interactions were statistically clearly associated with water temperature, species richness, and total eDNA concentration (GAMM, p < 0.05) except for the effects of species richness on the in-strengths.
source: The in-strengths and out-strengths of fish species interactions were statistically clearly associated with water temperature, species richness, and total eDNA concentration (GAMM, p < 0.05; Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1d) except for the effects on species richness on the in-strengths (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results from GAMM analysis showing relationships between interaction strengths and environmental variables.

claim: In-strengths of the fish–fish interactions increased with water temperature.
source: In-strengths of the fish–fish interactions increased with water temperature (Figure 3a), supporting our first hypothesis while out-strengths of the interactions showed an opposite pattern (Figure 3d), which might suggest there is a difference in the temperature dependence between the in-strengths and out-strengths of the interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between in-strengths and temperature, referencing a figure.

claim: Out-strengths of the fish–fish interactions showed an opposite pattern to in-strengths, decreasing with water temperature.
source: In-strengths of the fish–fish interactions increased with water temperature (Figure 3a), supporting our first hypothesis while out-strengths of the interactions showed an opposite pattern (Figure 3d), which might suggest there is a difference in the temperature dependence between the in-strengths and out-strengths of the interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between out-strengths and temperature, referencing a figure.

claim: Interaction strengths decreased with increasing species richness and total eDNA concentration.
source: Interaction strengths were also statistically clearly influenced by species richness and total eDNA concentrations (except for Figure 3b); the interaction strengths decreased with increasing species richness and total eDNA concentration.
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationships between interaction strengths and both species richness and total eDNA concentration.

claim: In-strengths of Halichoeres tenuispinis, Macrocanthus strigatus, Pempheris schwenkii, Stethojulis interrupta terina, and Thalassoma cupido clearly increased at higher water temperatures.
source: The in-strengths of several fish species clearly increased at higher water temperatures: for example, Halichoeres tenuispinis, Macrocanthus strigatus, Pempheris schwenkii, Stethojulis interrupta terina, and Thalassoma cupido (Figure 4a).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific species whose in-strengths increased with temperature, referencing a figure.

claim: In-strengths of Ditrema temminckii temminckii, Engraulis japonicus, and Girella punctata decreased at higher water temperatures.
source: On the other hand, in-strengths of some fish species and out-strengths decreased at higher water temperatures: for example, in-strengths of Ditrema temminckii temminckii, Engraulis japonicus, and Girella punctata, and out-strengths of five fish species (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific species whose in-strengths decreased with temperature, referencing a figure.

claim: Out-strengths of five fish species decreased at higher water temperatures.
source: On the other hand, in-strengths of some fish species and out-strengths decreased at higher water temperatures: for example, in-strengths of Ditrema temminckii temminckii, Engraulis japonicus, and Girella punctata, and out-strengths of five fish species (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: The manuscript states that out-strengths of five species decreased with temperature, referencing a figure.

claim: The relationship between the patterns of temperature and interaction strengths varies among fish species.
source: These results support our second hypothesis that the relationship between the patterns of temperature and interaction strengths varies among fish species.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states support for their second hypothesis based on the observed species-specific temperature effects.

claim: Approximately 83.3% of samples contain detectable concentrations of the standard DNA (Acanthopagrus schlegelii).
source: Approximately 83.3% of samples contain detectable concentrations of the standard DNA, which was used to convert sequence reads to eDNA copy numbers.
evidence: The manuscript states the percentage of samples containing the standard DNA, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MiSeq runs generated 71,892,685 reads in total for the eDNA samples.
source: We performed 21 MiSeq runs (with eDNA samples of other projects) to complete the analysis, which generated 71,892,685 reads in total for the eDNA samples of this project.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of sequencing reads generated.

claim: 98% of the reads were assigned to fish species.
source: Our multiple MiSeq runs generated 71,892,685 reads in total for the eDNA samples, of which 98% were assigned to fish species, and detected 1,130 MOTUs.
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of reads assigned to fish species.

claim: The eDNA metabarcoding initially detected 1,130 MOTUs before phylogenetic refinement.
source: Our multiple MiSeq runs generated 71,892,685 reads in total for the eDNA samples, of which 98% were assigned to fish species, and detected 1,130 MOTUs.
evidence: The manuscript reports the initial number of MOTUs detected before refinement.

claim: The study used a mixture of six primers (MiFish-U-forward, MiFish-U-reverse, MiFish-E-forward-v2, MiFish-E-reverse-v2, MiFish-U2-forward, and MiFish-U2-reverse) for the first-round PCR.
source: In the first-round PCR (1st PCR), we used a mixture of the following six primers: MiFish-U-forward, MiFish-U-reverse, MiFish-E-forward-v2, MiFish-E-reverse-v2, MiFish-U2-forward, and MiFish-U2-reverse (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript lists the specific primers used in the first PCR step.

claim: The MiFish primers amplified a hypervariable region of the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene of approximately 172 bp.
source: These primer pairs amplified a hypervariable region of the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene (ca. 172 bp; hereafter called the 'MiFish sequence') and appended primer-binding sites (5′ ends of the sequences before six random bases [Ns]) for sequencing at both ends of the amplicon.
evidence: The manuscript describes the target region and approximate size of the amplicon.

claim: Eight technical replicates were performed for the same eDNA template during the 1st PCR to minimize PCR dropouts.
source: To minimize PCR dropouts during the 1st PCR (Doi et al., 2019; Miya et al., 2020a), we performed eight technical replicates for the same eDNA template using a strip of eight tubes (200 µl).
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of technical replicates and cites previous studies justifying this approach.

claim: A total of 195 blanks were made and subjected to the library preparation procedure to monitor contamination (FB = 60, EB = 50, 1B = 50, 2B = 35).
source: In total, we made 195 blanks (FB = 60, EB = 50, 1B = 50, 2B = 35) and subjected them to the above library preparation procedure to monitor contamination during the on-site filtration, subsequent DNA extraction, and 1st and 2nd PCR of the 550 samples.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number and types of blank controls used.

claim: The rarefied ASV table resulted in 10,984,789 reads in total after rarefaction to approximately 20,000 reads per sample.
source: ASVs were rarefied to the approximate minimum read number (20,000), which resulted in 10,984,789 reads in total for the rarefied ASV table
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of reads after rarefaction.

claim: ASVs were subjected to taxon assignments to species names using the usearch global command with a sequence identity of >98.5% with the reference sequences and a query coverage of ≥90%.
source: ASVs were subjected to taxon assignments to species names (molecular operational taxonomic units; MOTUs) using the usearch global command with a sequence identity of >98.5% with the reference sequences (two nucleotide differences allowed) and a query coverage of ≥90%.
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific parameters used for taxonomic assignment.

claim: MiFish DB ver. 43 was used for taxon assignment, comprising 7973 species distributed across 464 families and 2675 genera.
source: MiFish DB ver. 43 was used for taxon assignment, comprising 7973 species distributed across 464 families and 2675 genera.
evidence: The manuscript specifies the reference database version and its contents.

claim: Reference sequences are currently available for about 70% of 4500 fish species in Japan.
source: At present, the reference sequences are available for about 70% of 4500 fish species in Japan.
evidence: The manuscript provides information on the coverage of the reference database for Japanese fish species.

claim: A total of 103 family-level trees were visually inspected for taxon assignment refinement.
source: A total of 103 family-level trees were visually inspected and taxon assignments were revised in the following manner.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of phylogenetic trees examined for taxonomic refinement.

claim: The primers and probe for qPCR were designed to specifically amplify a 129-bp fragment from the Acanthopagrus schlegelii mitochondrial cytochrome b gene.
source: The primers and probe were designed to specifically amplify a 129-bp fragment from the A. schlegelii mitochondrial cytochrome b (cyt b) gene (Takahashi et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the target region and size for the qPCR assay, citing the source of the primer design.

claim: The species specificity of the qPCR primers and probe was checked by Sasano et al., 2022.
source: The species specificity of the primers and probe was checked by Sasano et al., 2022.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study that validated the specificity of the primers and probe.

claim: No Acanthopagrus schlegelii DNA was detected from any FB, EB, or PCR blanks by qPCR.
source: We did not detect A. schlegelii DNA from any FB, EB, or PCR blanks by qPCR.
evidence: The manuscript reports the absence of contamination in blank samples as detected by qPCR.

claim: The converted ASV table included 23,863 detections.
source: The converted ASV table included 23,863 detections and we selected the top 50 most frequently detected species for our time series analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of detections in the converted ASV table.

claim: Seasonal changes in eDNA concentrations were consistent with the patterns of seasonal occurrences in tropical and subtropical fish species in the Boso Peninsula.
source: Seasonal changes in eDNA concentrations were consistent with the patterns of seasonal occurrences in tropical and subtropical fish species in the Boso Peninsula, to which they are transported by the warm Kuroshio Current, settling on the coastal waters during the warmer months and subsequently disappearing during the colder months (Saito, 2019; Senou et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript relates the observed eDNA patterns to known seasonal fish occurrence patterns, citing relevant studies.

claim: Pseudoblennius marmoratus and Pseudolabrus eoethinus have overlapping habitats and may interact.
source: The largest information flow was detected from Pseudoblennius marmoratus to Pseudolabrus eoethinus (Supplementary file 1c). These fish species have overlapping habitats, and thus, they may interact.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the detected information flow based on ecological knowledge of habitat overlap.

claim: Pseudolabrus eoethinus and Gymnothorax kidako are both carnivorous fish species and may conduct joint hunting.
source: Bidirectional information flow was detected between P. eoethinus and Gymnothorax kidako. They are both carnivorous fish species and may conduct joint hunting.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the bidirectional information flow based on the feeding ecology of the species.

claim: Chaenogobius annularis and Takifugu niphobles are often found together in the sand between reefs.
source: Chaenogobius annularis and Takifugu niphobles are often found together in the sand between reefs.
evidence: The manuscript states ecological knowledge about the co-occurrence of these species.

claim: Takifugu niphobles frequently dive in the sand, and benthos and mysids that are dug up during the dive may be prey for Chaenogobius annularis.
source: T. niphobles frequently dive in the sand, and benthos and mysids that are dug up during the dive may be prey for C. annularis.
evidence: The manuscript describes a potential ecological interaction based on the behavior of T. niphobles.

claim: The effects of salinity, tide and wave on interaction strengths were less clear, although the effects were statistically clear except for the effects of tide level on the out-strength.
source: The effects of salinity, tide and wave were less clear, although the effects were statistically clear except for the effects of tide level on the out-strength (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical clarity of effects of additional environmental variables, referencing a figure.

claim: Large variations in interaction strengths remained unexplained by environmental and ecological variables, suggesting that other factors may influence the interaction strengths.
source: Overall, environmental and ecological variables influenced the interaction strengths statistically clearly, but large variations remained unexplained (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3), suggesting that other factors (e.g., fish ecology, nutrient, and physiological status) may influence the interaction strengths.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges unexplained variation and speculates on potential additional factors.

claim: Water temperature may influence fish physiological activity such as feeding rates, growth rates, and swimming speed.
source: Previous studies showed that fish physiological activities, such as feeding rates, growth rates, and swimming speed, were influenced by water temperature (Claireaux et al., 2006; Kishi et al., 2005; Oyugi et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing temperature effects on fish physiology.

claim: The direction (positive or negative) of the temperature effects on fish metabolic activities may be species specific.
source: In addition, the direction (i.e., positive or negative) of the temperature effects on fish metabolic activities may be species specific (Oyugi et al., 2012), and this species specificity may underlie the species-specific effects of temperature on the interaction strength.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing species-specific temperature effects and infers implications for interaction strengths.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated that the quantity of eDNA may be a proxy of fish abundance and/or biomass.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that the quantity of eDNA may be a proxy of fish abundance and/or biomass (i.e., a positive correlation between the quantity of eDNA and fish abundance/biomass) (Takahara et al., 2012; Thomsen et al., 2012; Yamamoto et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies establishing the relationship between eDNA quantity and fish abundance/biomass.

claim: Species-specific differences in the copy numbers of the genetic marker and eDNA release rates do not cause serious biases in the reconstruction of networks and estimations of interaction strengths because time series are standardized before analysis.
source: Our nonlinear time series analysis used the information embedded in fluctuations in time series, and time series are always standardized before the analysis. Therefore, species-specific differences in the copy numbers of the genetic marker and eDNA release rates, which may bias the estimation of absolute abundance, do not cause serious biases in the reconstruction of the networks and estimations of interaction strengths.
evidence: The manuscript explains why certain biases do not affect their analysis due to standardization.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated that network reconstructions based on a time series analysis work reasonably well and show meaningful patterns.
source: Although previous studies demonstrated that network reconstructions based on a time series analysis work reasonably well and show meaningful patterns (Runge et al., 2019; Sugihara et al., 2012; Ushio, 2022a; Ushio et al., 2018a), experiment/observation-based validations of the reconstructed network have not yet been performed.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies supporting the validity of time series-based network reconstruction.

claim: Experiment/observation-based validations of the reconstructed network have not yet been performed.
source: Although previous studies demonstrated that network reconstructions based on a time series analysis work reasonably well and show meaningful patterns (Runge et al., 2019; Sugihara et al., 2012; Ushio, 2022a; Ushio et al., 2018a), experiment/observation-based validations of the reconstructed network have not yet been performed.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation in the validation of their network reconstruction approach.

claim: The advantages of the eDNA method include low cost and minimal time and labor needed for field sampling as well as the potential scalability of the library preparation process.
source: Nonetheless, the advantages of the eDNA method are the low cost and minimal time and labor needed for field sampling as well as the potential scalability of the library preparation process (Ushio et al., 2022c).
evidence: The manuscript describes advantages of the eDNA method, citing a relevant study.

claim: Water temperature and oxygen concentration covary and both directly/indirectly affect fish physiology.
source: For example, water temperature and oxygen concentration covary and both directly/indirectly affect fish physiology (Salvatteci et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing the covariation of temperature and oxygen and their effects on fish physiology.

claim: Temperature plays an important role in determining fish body size at the historical time scale.
source: Recent studies have shown that temperature (and oxygen) plays an important role in determining fish body size at the historical time scale (Salvatteci et al., 2022; Yasuhara and Deutsch, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent studies showing temperature effects on fish body size over historical time scales.

claim: Fish body size plays a critical role in interspecific interactions such as predator–prey interactions.
source: As fish body size plays a critical role in interspecific interactions such as predator–prey interactions (e.g., predator–prey mass ratio; Nakazawa et al., 2011), temperature-induced body size changes may influence interspecific interactions at a longer time scale.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing the importance of body size in predator-prey interactions.

claim: Temperature may induce changes in fish–fish interactions at a relatively short time scale (weeks to months), perhaps via temperature effects on the physiological activity of fish individuals.
source: On the other hand, our study showed that temperature may induce changes in fish–fish interactions at a relatively short time scale (weeks to months), perhaps via temperature effects on the physiological activity of fish individuals.
evidence: The manuscript describes their findings on short-term temperature effects and proposes a mechanism.

claim: Increased water temperature strengthens interactions received by Halichoeres tenuispinis and Microcanthus strigatus, which may destabilize the population dynamics of these species.
source: For example, increased water temperature strengthens interactions received by H. tenuispinis and M. strigatus (Figure 4), which may destabilize the population dynamics of these species.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temperature effect on specific species and infers potential consequences for population dynamics.

claim: Increased water temperature may exert opposite effects on Engraulis japonicus and Girella punctata, resulting in weakened interactions and stabilized population dynamics.
source: In contract, increased water temperature may exert the opposite effects on E. japonicus and G. punctata (Figure 4), that is, weakened interactions and stabilized population dynamics.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temperature effect on specific species and infers potential consequences for population dynamics.

claim: The dominance of weak interactions stabilizes the dynamics of a natural fish community.
source: The dominance of weak interactions stabilizes the dynamics of a natural fish community (Ushio et al., 2018a).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing the stabilizing effect of weak interactions.

claim: Interaction strengths have been reported to decrease with increases in the diversity of experimental microbial communities.
source: Interaction strengths have been reported to decrease with increases in the diversity of experimental microbial communities (Ratzke et al., 2020), and this holds true even for more diverse ecological communities under field conditions (Ushio, 2022a).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing the relationship between diversity and interaction strength in different systems.

claim: Coley and Aide, 1991 proposed that interactions between plants and insect herbivores were generally stronger in warmer regions.
source: In terrestrial ecosystems, Coley and Aide, 1991 proposed that interactions between plants and insect herbivores were generally stronger in warmer regions, which may result in stronger negative density dependence for tree species and contribute to higher plant diversity in a tropical region (Forrister et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study proposing stronger plant-herbivore interactions in warmer regions.

claim: Wieczynski et al., 2021 showed that species-level functional traits (e.g., body size and shape) may underlie the relationships between temperature and interaction strengths.
source: In addition, Wieczynski et al., 2021 showed that species-level functional traits (e.g., body size and shape) may underlie the relationships between temperature and interaction strengths.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing the role of functional traits in temperature-interaction strength relationships.

claim: Most studies evaluating the effects of temperature on interaction strengths of marine organisms have been performed targeting relatively immobile or small organisms or under laboratory conditions.
source: Although many studies have evaluated the effects of temperature on interaction strengths of marine organisms (Kordas et al., 2011), most of these studies have been performed targeting relatively immobile or small organisms (Bertness and Ewanchuk, 2002; Chen et al., 2012) or under laboratory conditions (e.g., mesocosm experiments; Allan et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies and characterizes their scope and limitations.

claim: It currently remains unclear how temperature influences the strengths of interspecific interactions of larger, more mobile marine organisms, such as fish, under field conditions.
source: While the previous studies have provided invaluable information, it currently remains unclear how temperature influences the strengths of interspecific interactions of larger, more mobile marine organisms, such as fish, which may exert strong top-down regulations on ecological communities, especially under field condition.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a knowledge gap in the literature regarding temperature effects on fish interactions in the field.

claim: Recent studies demonstrated that eDNA metabarcoding combined with frequent water sampling enabled the efficient monitoring of high-diversity ecological communities.
source: Recent studies demonstrated that eDNA metabarcoding combined with frequent water sampling enabled the efficient monitoring of high-diversity ecological communities (Bista et al., 2017; Djurhuus et al., 2020; Ushio, 2022a).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies demonstrating the effectiveness of frequent eDNA sampling for biodiversity monitoring.

claim: If eDNA metabarcoding is performed quantitatively (e.g., by including spike-in DNAs), the data may contain information on species abundance.
source: Furthermore, if eDNA metabarcoding is performed quantitatively (e.g., by including spike-in DNAs; Ushio et al., 2018b), these data may contain information on species abundance.
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing that quantitative eDNA metabarcoding can provide abundance information.

claim: Recent studies have shown that information on interspecific interactions may be embedded in multispecies eDNA time series, particularly when the data are 'quantitative'.
source: More importantly, recent studies have shown that information on interspecific interactions may be embedded in multispecies eDNA time series, particularly when the data are 'quantitative' (Ushio, 2022a).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing that quantitative eDNA time series can contain information about interactions.

claim: Transfer entropy (TE) is a method based on the information theory that quantifies information flow between two variables.
source: For example, transfer entropy (TE) is a method based on the information theory that quantifies information flow between two variables (Runge et al., 2012; Schreiber, 2000).
evidence: The manuscript describes transfer entropy and cites foundational studies.

claim: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) is a causality detection tool in empirical dynamic modeling.
source: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) is a causality detection tool in empirical dynamic modeling (Sugihara et al., 2012), which is based on the dynamical theory.
evidence: The manuscript describes CCM and cites the foundational study.

claim: TE and CCM have more recently been understood under the information theory framework, and unified information-theoretic causality (UIC) may also quantify information flow between variables.
source: TE and CCM have more recently been understood under the information theory framework, and unified information-theoretic causality (UIC) may also quantify information flow between variables (Osada et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study unifying TE and CCM under an information theory framework.

claim: The multiview distance regularized (MDR) S-map enables accurate quantifications of interaction strengths of a large interaction network even when the number of network nodes exceeds the time series length.
source: In addition, an improved version of a sequentially weighted global linear map (S-map), called the multiview distance regularized (MDR) S-map, enables accurate quantifications of interaction strengths of a large interaction network even when the number of network nodes exceeds the time series length (Chang et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript describes the MDR S-map method and cites the study that developed it.

claim: The interactions detected by the time series analysis should have a time scale of twice a month (the sampling frequency), meaning the study tends to focus on behavior-level interactions rather than birth–death processes.
source: As our eDNA time series was taken twice a month, the interactions detected should also have the same time scale (e.g., the interactions detected may cause changes in the population size at the same time scale), which means that we tend to focus on behavior-level interactions (e.g., feeding, vigilance, and schooling) rather than birth–death process in the present study (except for predation).
evidence: The manuscript explains the temporal resolution of their analysis and its implications for the types of interactions detected.

claim: The interactions detected by the time series analysis could include various types of interactions such as competition and mutualism that could be involved in the population dynamics.
source: In addition, the interactions we detected by the time series analysis could include various types of interactions such as competition and mutualism that could be involved in the population dynamics.
evidence: The manuscript describes the potential types of interactions that could be detected by their analysis.

claim: The study hypothesized that a positive relationship exists between temperature and interaction strengths at the community level.
source: We hypothesized that (1) a positive relationship exists between temperature and interaction strengths at the community level, as found in other ecosystems and many types of interactions
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states their first hypothesis.

claim: The study hypothesized that the relationship between the patterns of temperature and interaction strengths varies among fish species because of species-specific ecologies and behavior.
source: and (2) the relationship between the patterns of temperature and interaction strengths varies among fish species because of species-specific ecologies and the behavior of component species.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states their second hypothesis.

claim: The study sites are located within or surrounded by rocky shores with intricate coastlines.
source: The 11 stations are located within or surrounded by rocky shores with intricate coastlines.
evidence: The manuscript describes the habitat characteristics of the study sites.

claim: The northernmost stations on both sides (Sts. 1 and 11) are markedly affected by the cold Oyashio Current and inner-bay water from Tokyo Bay, respectively.
source: The northernmost stations on both sides (Sts. 1 and 11) are markedly affected by the cold Oyashio Current (Yang et al., 1993) and inner-bay water from Tokyo Bay (Fujiwara and Yamada, 2002), respectively
evidence: The manuscript describes the oceanographic influences on specific study sites, citing relevant studies.

claim: The remaining stations (Sts. 2–10) are markedly affected by the warm Kuroshio Current flowing northward along the Pacific coast as well as its branches.
source: while the remaining stations (Sts. 2–10) are markedly affected by the warm Kuroshio Current flowing northward along the Pacific coast as well as its branches (Soh, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript describes the oceanographic influences on most study sites, citing a relevant study.

claim: Water temperature has significant influences on marine community composition and diversity at the global spatial scale and historical time scale.
source: Water temperature has significant influences on marine community composition and diversity at the global spatial scale and historical time scale (Tittensor et al., 2010; Yasuhara and Deutsch, 2023)
